title: Philippine Immigration Detention: If You Don't Pay, Your Deportation Never Moves
dek: A Chinese surfer was held in the Philippines for 41 days. What he saw wasn't a prison — it was a business with a price list: beds, boxed meals, phones, lawyer fees, every item bought with cash. Those who don't pay stay locked up for years, even decades.
why: StoryFM's Behind Bars series. Medium information density but solid detail. The first half is one man's ordeal; the second half — the gang economy inside the detention center, the ransom quotes from scam companies, the lawyers who jack up prices on the spot — is where the real value is.
who: Founders and overseas-expansion practitioners interested in the situation of Chinese abroad, the Philippine business environment, and the machinery of gray-industry and immigration corruption.
skip: 6:29-9:14 — surfing history and startup background, unrelated to the core mechanism.

points.h: The Immigration Bureau quoted 1.5 million pesos to walk free on the spot
points.body: The night Feili was arrested, an Immigration Bureau officer pulled him aside and whispered, "I can help you." After talking to a lawyer, the answer came back: hand over 1.5 million pesos, roughly 160,000-170,000 RMB, and you walk immediately, no problem at all. Of the 12 to 13 people arrested in the same sweep, nobody agreed to pay. Everyone thought it was impossible that such a thing could still exist in 2026, and wanted to resolve it through normal legal channels. The price of refusing: they were transferred from the holding cells of the General Santos police station to the Immigration Bureau detention center in Manila, where Feili ultimately spent 41 days.

points.h: When his phone was confiscated, the money in Gcash was transferred out
points.body: When Feili was detained his phone was taken, and they asked for his unlock code. He assumed it was standard procedure and gave it. His phone unlock code was the same as his Gcash payment password — the Philippine equivalent of Alipay. For the next four or five days he applied repeatedly and could not get the phone back, until he kept pressing the Chinese consulate and a lawyer, and it was finally returned. When he turned it on, the interface had all switched to English, and the Gcash transfer history showed money had been sent out — then sent back the night before he got the phone. There was only about 1,000 RMB in it. Feili says it wasn't about the amount; it was that someone had touched it while it wasn't in his hands. His read: many Chinese in Manila doing gray-industry scams go through this same shakedown after arrest, but they don't dare go to the Chinese consulate, because their phones are full of criminal evidence.

points.h: The air conditioning and takeout the Immigration Bureau promised exist — in another form
points.body: For those unwilling to buy their own tickets to transfer, the Immigration Bureau works on them in shifts, saying conditions at the Manila bureau are excellent: air conditioning, plenty of freedom, a gym, basketball, takeout delivery, phone use. Feili says they weren't lying — there really is air conditioning, you really can order takeout, it's just another form, a completely different form. They arrived at the main detention center at past three in the morning. What he saw after getting off the vehicle was a square area wrapped in a layer of iron grating, under a sheet-metal roof, ringed by dog-cage-like iron cells, inside them long communal platforms, several hundred people. At past three in the morning many weren't sleeping — bare-chested, in nothing but underwear, they clung to the iron cages staring at the newcomers. Feili says he and the other foreigners didn't speak for several minutes after getting off, then it hit them: the Immigration Bureau had lied to them.

points.h: The detention center is a business invested in by a Chinese boss
points.body: What Feili heard inside was that this Immigration Bureau detention center was invested in by a Chinese boss, in cooperation with the bureau, and that the beds, toilets and other facilities were all newly built by that Chinese boss. Foreigners just stay, but Chinese who come in have to pay. The cheapest communal-platform bed is 10,000 pesos a month, about 1,100-1,200 RMB. Wealthy pan bosses and gambling kingpins can pay 50,000 pesos a month, over 6,000 RMB, for a so-called "air-conditioned room" — actually the same bed, just wrapped in tin foil and wooden boards, with a styrofoam box of ice beside it, a hole cut in the box, and an exhaust fan drawing the cold air into the bed. That is where the Immigration Bureau's promise of "air conditioning inside" came from.

points.h: Chinese gangs collect protection money: you want out without paying?
points.body: On Feili's first day inside, the head of the Chinese gang came to collect a "rumor fee," saying the facilities were their investment and there was no way to stay for free. Feili said he had no money, he was here to serve time, how could he be expected to pay on top of that. The gang boss, threatening, said: you're already in and you don't want to spend money, and you still think you're getting out? Feili learned that the place is run by gangs, and the Chinese gang monopolizes all food, clothing and daily life for Chinese — running a Chinese restaurant and a Chinese supermarket. The whole detention center holds about 200 people; when Feili arrived it was the slow season, and Chinese numbered over 100, more than half of them gambling and gray industry. The Chinese gang's staff draw wages — the head chef 10,000 pesos a month, the kitchen helper 5,000 pesos. The pay is very low, but many can't get out precisely because they have no money for a lawyer, so they can only work to earn.

points.h: A Yunnan man held over a year; his family thought he died in Southeast Asia
points.body: A young man from Yunnan asked Feili for help. Before the pandemic he'd been lured to the Philippines by a high-salary recruitment ad; the moment he landed his phone and passport were taken, and he was pulled into a park to do telecom fraud. With poor numbers he was shocked with an electric baton by his supervisor every day. After the company was busted he served a few months, then was transferred to the Immigration Bureau detention center. The normal deportation procedure is simple — a few departments sign off, you buy your own ticket, and you go — but the Immigration Bureau, to extract money, keeps you locked up a long time, and without paying the procedure doesn't move. He'd already been held over a year, with not a cent, no phone, eating only prison food every day, unable to reach his family, who thought he had died in Southeast Asia. Feili helped him write a letter in Chinese, translated it into English, and through an introduction from a Japanese man got to see the warden, who had a guard bring Feili's phone so the young man could add his father on WeChat and send a selfie and a voice message. Afterward the Immigration Bureau bought a basic phone specifically to solve this problem.

points.h: Scam company ransom: 3 million pesos per person
points.body: The only Chinese Feili talked with much came from a scam company. The company's 70 or 80 people were surrounded by the Immigration Bureau together with the police and the NBI, three agencies. The first shakedown: the NBI and police locked each person in a toilet — no cameras there — and took everything valuable off them. The second: the Immigration Bureau negotiated ransoms with the company boss, a different quote per person, 1 million, 2 million, 3 million pesos, depending on the person in charge's mood. That company settled at 3 million pesos per person, over 300,000 RMB. The boss ultimately ransomed 30 people — exactly the 30 held on one floor — and the rest were promised food deliveries until release. This young man ran an operation targeting the Japanese market, scamming middle-aged Japanese women; his best month brought in 2 million RMB, and he bought a house and a car in his home county. Later he was kidnapped by a friend, had several hundred thousand transferred away, and was hit with a false illegal-possession-of-firearms charge by a corrupt cop, so he couldn't leave.

points.h: A Philippine lawyer raises the price on the spot when he sees you're Chinese
points.body: In Cebu, through an introduction from a Lithuanian, Feili met a Philippine lawyer who quoted 200,000 pesos, over 20,000 RMB, done in four weeks. After Feili reached Manila the lawyer came to visit, saw he was Chinese, and immediately raised the price, saying the earlier figure was the old price and the new price required another 120,000 pesos, over 10,000 RMB. Feili decided not to use him and wrote off the deposit, turning instead to a Chinese middleman. The Chinese middleman quoted over 30,000 RMB, four to six weeks, no more than six. Feili says the truly reliable Chinese middlemen know this procedure inside out, because everyone locked up in there is Chinese. In the end he was held over 30 days there, 41 days including Cebu. The Lithuanian who introduced the Philippine lawyer still hadn't gotten out when Feili messaged him.
